sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: Exidia nigricans forms rubbery, gelatinous basidiomata, dark sepia to black. Small buttons merge into an irregular, lobed, often brain-like mass, typically 5 to 15 cm across. The upper hymenial surface is shiny when wet and dotted with small pegs; the fungus attaches directly to wood, with no cap or stem.

sections.title: Moisture and useful characters
sections.text: In dry weather, the lobes shrivel and may form a dark warty crust; they swell and regain their gelatinous texture when rehydrated. The spore print is white and the spores are allantoid, meaning curved like a sausage, but these microscopic characters are not visible in the plate.

sections.title: Substrate and season
sections.text: This saprotroph grows on dead broad-leaved wood, including beech, ash and hazel; some sources report oak less often. It can fruit throughout the year depending on climate and is most conspicuous in autumn, winter and early spring.

sections.title: Lookalikes and caution
sections.text: Exidia glandulosa is very similar, and the boundary between the two taxa has a history of confusion; some checklists and studies still discuss their distinction. In the concept used by British sources, E. nigricans forms fused, lobed masses, while E. glandulosa tends to have separate top-shaped cushions. It has no established culinary value; do not eat it.

traits: Dark sepia to black gelatinous mass made of fused, brain-like lobes
Wet upper surface shiny and dotted with small pegs
Shrivels into a dark warty crust in dry weather and swells again when wet
Basidioma attached directly to dead wood, without cap, stem, gills or pores
Dead broad-leaved wood, including beech, ash and hazel · year-round, most visible autumn to early spring
Similar to Exidia glandulosa; historical and taxonomic separation should be treated cautiously
safetyNote: A gelatinous reference fungus with no established culinary value. This entry does not recommend consumption.
